topics.title: Underground Construction
topics.description: PVC conduit, sweeps, glue, and common mistakes
topics.intro: Underground work is common in outdoor and site lighting. PVC is the go-to raceway. Get the joints right and the inspector will move on fast.

cards.title: PVC Conduit Basics
list: PVC is the standard for underground electrical raceway
Schedule 40 vs Schedule 80: 80 has thicker walls (more protection)
Use expansion fittings where PVC enters a building or structure
PVC expands and contracts with temperature — long runs need expansion fittings every ~100 ft
body: Schedule 80 is required where subject to physical damage (above ground transitions).
cards.remember: Schedule 80 where exposed — Schedule 40 underground.

cards.title: PVC Couplings & Connectors
list: Coupling: joins two pieces of conduit in a straight run
Bell end: factory-expanded end — no coupling needed
Terminal adapter: threaded PVC to male/female connections at boxes
Female adapter: threads onto a threaded hub
Male adapter: threads into a female hub or box
cards.remember: Glue couplings fully — quarter turn when seating.

cards.title: PVC Sweeps (Bends)
list: Pre-formed sweeps come in 90°, 45°, 30°, 22.5°, and 15°
Radius matters: larger radius = easier pull
Common radius: 2" PVC 90° sweep ≈ 24" radius
Maximum of 360° total bends between pull boxes (NEC 300.34)
NEVER field-bend PVC with heat unless you know what you're doing — use factory sweeps for underground
cards.remember: Factory sweeps pull easier than field-bent PVC.

cards.title: Primer & Glue (Solvent Welding)
body: Purple primer cleans and softens PVC for bonding — required by code for a visible joint.
Apply primer to both surfaces (pipe OD and coupling ID).
Apply PVC cement to both surfaces immediately after primer.
Assemble with a QUARTER TURN (1/4 twist) to distribute glue evenly.
Hold for 15-30 seconds to prevent push-out.
Wipe off excess — sloppy glue fails inspection.
list: Purple primer = inspector can see you did it right
Grey cement for PVC schedule 40/80
Blue cement for CPVC (hot environments)
cards.remember: Primer first, glue second, quarter turn, hold 15 seconds.

cards.title: Expansion Fittings
list: Required where PVC enters a building or structure
Allows for thermal expansion/contraction
Install at transitions from underground to above ground
Split coupling or telescoping type
Position in middle of straight run, not near boxes
cards.remember: Underground PVC moves with temperature — expansion fittings prevent buckling.

cards.title: PVC Support & Backfill
list: Trench bottom: 4-6" of compacted sand or gravel bedding
PVC supported every 3-4 ft in trench, no large rocks directly against pipe
Backfill first 12" with sand or sifted dirt — no sharp rocks
Warning tape placed 12" above conduit
Tamp in 6" lifts — settling causes problems later
cards.remember: Sand bedding + warning tape = happy inspector.

cards.title: Common Underground Mistakes
list: Using standard PVC glue without primer — instant fail
No expansion fitting at building transition
Too many bends (over 360°) between pull boxes
Sharp rocks in backfill cutting conduit later
No warning tape or tracer wire
Sch 40 where Sch 80 required (above ground transitions)
Glue joints not held long enough — push-out leaks
cards.remember: Every mistake above is a callback that costs more than doing it right the first time.

cards.title: Underground Pull Boxes & Handholes
list: Required where conduit changes direction or needs access
Must be accessible — not buried or paved over
Minimum size: longest pull + 6" for straight pulls (NEC 314.28)
Angle pulls: 6× raceway + all entries
Handholes for site lighting are common — specify rated cover for traffic
cards.remember: Too few pull boxes = nightmare pull that damages wire.

cards.title: Bell Ends & Terminations

rows: Expanded PVC end — eliminates coupling in straight runs
Male threads for boxes with female hubs

cards.remember: Bell ends save couplings on long straight runs — use them.

cards.title: PVC Trenching Tips
list: Call 811 before ANY digging — minimum 48 hours notice
Minimum cover: 18" for residential (NEC 300.5)
24" under driveways and parking areas
Trench width: pipe OD + 4" minimum on each side
Glue joints BEFORE placing in trench when possible
Wait 30 min for glue to cure before backfill in cold weather
cards.remember: Depth, bedding, tape, and cure time — four things inspectors check.

topics.title: Wire Pulling Masterclass
topics.description: Rope, fish tape, lubricant, and communication
topics.intro: Pulling wire seems simple until you have 500 ft of 500 kcmil with three 90s. Proper technique saves your back and the wire.

cards.title: Pulling Methods Overview

rows: Holding all conductors at pulling end

cards.remember: Match the method to the run — fish tape is not for 4/0 feeders.

cards.title: Fish Tape Technique
list: Push fish tape through from pull end to feed end
Always push with the reel, not the tape end
Keep tension on the tape as you push — prevents birdnesting
Use a leader or bullet tip to navigate bends
Never force past a bend — you may be stabbing insulation
Lube helps even with fish tape
body: Pro tip: put a 90° hook on the tape end for turning corners.
cards.remember: Push the reel, not the tape — and keep it taught.

cards.title: Pull Rope (Polypropylene)
list: Poly rope is cheap, strong, and floats on lube
Blow or fish a pull line through first, then attach pulling rope
Use a swivel to prevent rope twist transferring to wire
Tie a proper knot: figure-8 or bowline on a coil
Mark rope every 50 ft with tape for distance reference
Never use rope as a permanent support for wire
cards.remember: Pull rope first — then attach wire. Never pull wire directly with fish tape on long runs.

cards.title: Wire Lubricant
list: Lubricant reduces friction by 50%+ on long pulls
Types: water-based soap, gel, slippery polymer
Apply generously at head end and every pull box along the way
Pour lube into conduit before pushing wire in
Use a lube pump or spray for best coverage
More lube = less pulling tension = less damage
cards.remember: Lube is cheaper than replacing damaged wire — use it liberally.

cards.title: Staggering Conductors
list: When pulling multiple conductors, stagger the ends at different lengths (6-12" apart)
Staggering makes the pulling head more aerodynamic through bends
All conductors enter the bend at different times — reduces binding
Mark each conductor at the pull end with phase tape before starting
body: Cut conductors in a staircase pattern at the pulling end — not all the same length.
cards.remember: Staggered head = smoother pull through conduit.

cards.title: Pulling Commands & Communication
list: "READY?" — puller asks if feed end is ready
"PULLING" — puller starts pulling slowly
"HOLD" — stop pulling immediately, hold position
"STOP" — stop and release tension
"TAKE TENSION" — feeder person pulls slack out before puller pulls
"READY FOR MORE" — feeder has more wire to feed
Establish clear verbal commands BEFORE starting the pull
cards.remember: Communication saves fingers and wire — agree on commands before you pull.

cards.title: Cable Tugger Operation
list: Set up tugger in line with conduit — avoid side pulls
Check max pull rating on tugger — do not exceed
Use pulling socks (wire mesh grips) for multiple conductors
Monitor tension gauge — if it spikes, STOP and investigate
Pull speed: slow and steady — fast pulling heats wire
Anchor the tugger securely — 2,000 lbs+ of force can move an unsecured tugger
cards.remember: Tugger pulls are powerful — respect the tension gauge.

cards.title: Maximum Pulling Tension
body: Max tension = 0.008 × circular mil area of each conductor.
For multiple conductors in parallel, multiply by number of conductors.
cards.remember: If it feels like too much tension, it probably is — stop and investigate.

cards.title: Pulling Socks & Grips
list: Mesh pulling grip slides over conductor bundle
Kellems grip for multiple conductors (woven wire mesh)
Wrap mesh tight — tape over the end to prevent snagging
Never exceed the grip's rated pulling tension
Inspect grip for broken wires before each use
Use a swivel between rope and grip to prevent twisting
cards.remember: A failed pulling sock mid-conduit is a nightmare — inspect every time.

cards.title: Preventing Wire Damage
list: Wire damage = nicked insulation, stretched conductors, broken strands
Use proper size pulling eye or basket grip
Keep wire off the ground to avoid dirt/grit embedding in insulation
Smooth out sharp edges at pull boxes (use bushings or rollers)
Never pull wire across sharp edges without protection
Check insulation integrity after pull with megger on critical runs
cards.remember: Damaged wire fails early and always at the worst time.

topics.title: Material Identification
topics.description: LB, LL, LR, condulets, and more
topics.intro: Electricians speak in part numbers. Knowing a 'C-condulet' from a 'Meyers hub' by sight saves trips to the supply house.

cards.title: Conduit Bodies (Condulets) Overview
list: Conduit bodies are access fittings for pulling wire at direction changes
Types: LB, LL, LR, C, T, X — letter tells you the entry pattern
LB = L body with a back (rear) opening
LL = L body with left opening
LR = L body with right opening
C = straight-through body
T = T-body with three entries
X = cross body with four entries
body: The letter indicates the configuration: L = 90° turn, and the last letter tells you where the cover/access is (B=back, L=left, R=right).
cards.remember: LB = L-body Back. LL = L-body Left. LR = L-body Right.

cards.title: Meyers Hubs (Watertight Connectors)
list: Meyers hub = watertight sealing hub for rigid/IMC conduit entering enclosures
Used on outdoor enclosures, panel tops, and weatherproof boxes
Has an O-ring seal and locknut — install on the box before conduit
Two types: standard and insulated throat (protects wire)
Torque to spec — overtightening damages seal
Look for the neoprene gasket — signs of a proper seal
cards.remember: Meyers hub = weatherproof entry — O-ring must be visible after install.

cards.title: Bushings & Inserts

rows: Threads onto end of rigid/IMC — protects wire from sharp edges
Has plastic ring inside — protects THHN insulation from cuts
Reduces from larger to smaller hub size
Has a lug for bonding — used at service equipment
Secures conduit into box or enclosure

cards.remember: Insulated bushing on every THHN pull — prevents wire chafing.

cards.title: Beam Clamps & Strut Fittings

rows: Attaches to steel beam — supports conduit hangers
Metal channel for mounting everything — panels, conduit, trays
Slides into strut channel — holds bolts at any position
Clamps conduit to strut or beam

cards.remember: Strut is the erector set of electrical construction — learn all the fittings.

cards.title: All-Thread Rod & Hardware
list: All-thread (threaded rod): used to suspend trapeze, strut racks, and panels
Use with beam clamps, nuts, washers, and strut
Cut with hacksaw or reciprocating saw — deburr threading end
Double-nut: lock two nuts together to prevent vibration loosening
cards.remember: All-thread + strut + beam clamps = the backbone of overhead mounts.

cards.title: Ground Rods & Clamps
list: Ground rod: 8 ft copper-clad or galvanized steel
Drive full length — only 2-4" above grade
Ground rod clamp: bronze or brass, connects GEC to rod
Acorn clamp: single bolt for easy install
Split bolt: for tapping ground conductors
Two rods required if first rod tests > 25Ω (NEC 250.56)
Rods at least 6 ft apart
cards.remember: Rod goes in full length — clamp above grade for inspection.

cards.title: Pull Boxes & Junction Boxes

rows: Access point for pulling wire — large, often no devices
Splices and connections — must remain accessible
Underground access box — rated for traffic load
Adds depth when box is too shallow
Raises device up to finished wall surface

cards.remember: All boxes must remain accessible — never bury a junction box.

cards.title: Conduit Straps & Supports

rows: Heavy support for rigid, large pipe
Hangs conduit from strut or beam

cards.remember: Support EMT every 10 ft and within 3 ft of every box.

cards.title: Pole Bases & Outdoor Distribution
list: Pole base: concrete foundation for light pole
Must have pull box (handhole) adjacent to pole base
Anchor bolts cast in concrete — template critical
Ground lug in pole base for bonding pole to GEC
PVC stub-up through concrete base to pole interior
Seal conduit entry to pole — prevents water ingress
cards.remember: Pole lighting = pole base + handhole + ground + sealed entry.

cards.title: Service Entrance Hardware

rows: Top of service riser — protects drop from weather
Rigid conduit that holds weatherhead and service drop
Enclosure for utility meter — belongs to utility
Switch that shuts off all building power
Terminate wires at meter, panel, or disconnect

cards.remember: Service hardware is utility-specific — verify with local requirements.

topics.title: Tape Measure & Fractions
topics.description: Master every mark on the tape
topics.intro: Fractions mess up more apprentices than voltage calculations. Learn the tape measure cold and you will never cut a stud short again.

cards.title: The Tape Measure Anatomy
list: Hook: loose rivets let it slide for inside/outside measurements
Blade: curved shape keeps it rigid when extended
Standout: distance blade extends without support (longer = better)
Belt clip: keep it on your tool belt at all times
Markings: 1/16, 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, inch — 16 marks per inch
cards.remember: Every inch has 16 marks — the hook end slides 1/16" for accuracy.

cards.title: Reading 16ths (Every Mark)
cards.remember: The longest mark = inch. 2nd longest = 1/2". 3rd longest = 1/4". Shortest = 1/16".

cards.title: Adding & Subtracting Fractions (Field Method)
list: 36" + 1/4" = 36-1/4" — write it as a mixed number
1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4 — common denominator is always 16 in field work
Favorite trick: measure to nearest 1/16 and add the remainder
Pro trick: use the tape itself to add/subtract — mark, then align
cards.remember: When adding fractions: convert to /16 first, then add normally.

cards.title: Marking Strategies
list: V-notch: razor knife V-mark for precise alignment
Pencil line: thin line across the mark
Chalk line: long straight lines for conduit and layout
Fence: use a square scrap as a guide for repetitive cuts
Burn an inch: measure from 1" mark and subtract 1" to avoid worn hook
cards.remember: Sharp pencil + straight edge = accurate cut.

cards.title: Common Tape Measure Mistakes
list: Reading the wrong mark (counting 1/4 marks instead of 1/2)
Forgetting the hook slides 1/16" (inside vs outside measurement)
Not accounting for blade bend on long horizontal spans
Misreading 3/4" as 5/8" — look closely at the mark height
Cutting conduit 1/2" too long because you read 10" instead of 10-1/2"
cards.remember: Check twice, read aloud, cut once.

cards.title: Mental Math for Fractions
list: 1/2" = 8/16" — always your reference
5/8 = 10/16 — useful for adding
3/4" is 12/16" — three 1/4" marks from the inch
If you can count to 16, you can read a tape
cards.remember: 16/16 = 1 — memorize the 16s and you'll never guess.

topics.title: Bucket Trucks & Rigging
topics.description: Spotter duties, outriggers, fall protection, and hand signals
topics.intro: Bucket trucks and rigging go together on outdoor lighting jobs. Safety is non-negotiable — one mistake can kill.

cards.title: Bucket Truck Pre-Operation Checks
list: Check hydraulic fluid level
Inspect boom for cracks, damage, or leaks
Verify outriggers deploy and lock properly
Test emergency lowering system
Check tires and air pressure
Verify all safety decals are present and readable
Inspect harness and lanyard for wear
Never operate if any safety device is disabled
cards.remember: Daily pre-check takes 5 minutes — skipping it costs lives.

cards.title: Spotter Duties
list: Spotter watches boom clearance at all times
Maintains visual contact with operator in bucket
Keeps people and equipment clear of work area
Communicates with hand signals if voice fails
Watches for power lines, trees, building edges
Responsible for stopping operation immediately if unsafe
NEVER leave the spotter position while the boom is elevated
cards.remember: The spotter is the operator's eyes on the ground — never distracted.

cards.title: Outrigger Setup
list: Deploy outriggers on stable, level ground
Use outrigger pads on asphalt, dirt, or grass (never directly on soft ground)
Extend to full width — narrower stance = less stable
Level the truck using bubble indicator before extending boom
Chock wheels on slopes even with outriggers deployed
Lock outriggers in position — verify pinned
cards.remember: Outriggers on pads + truck level + locked = stable platform.

cards.title: Fall Protection in Bucket
list: Full-body harness with D-ring in center of back
Lanyard attached to designated bucket anchor point (not the boom)
Never climb out of the bucket — use it ONLY from inside
Keep both feet on bucket floor
No leaning over bucket edge — reposition instead
Self-retracting lanyard for fall arrest
100% tie-off: always connected to something
cards.remember: Harness on before you leave the ground — no exceptions.

cards.title: Minimum Approach Distances (MAD)
body: These are OSHA minimums — many companies have stricter limits.
Add 4 ft for non-rated workers near power lines.
cards.remember: 10 ft for 50kV and under — if unsure, stay farther.

cards.title: Traffic Safety (Work Zone Setup)
list: Cones and signs: warn drivers 500 ft+ before work area
Flaggers with stop/slow paddles when lane is affected
Vests: Class 2 or 3 hi-vis reflective
Truck with arrow board facing traffic
Park truck between work area and traffic as barrier
Never turn your back to traffic — always face oncoming
Use hand signals — horn blast for emergency stop
cards.remember: Traffic kills more workers than electricity — respect the zone.

cards.title: Rigging Slings & Hardware

rows: Heavy lifts — conforms to load shape
Bent pin, cracked body, thread damage

cards.remember: Inspect every sling before use — damaged rigging kills.

cards.title: Tag Lines & Load Control
list: Tag line = rope attached to load for directional control
Never stand under a suspended load
Keep tag line taut — prevents load spinning
Use on all crane and boom truck picks
Clear the area of non-essential personnel before lift
Communication: hand signals between rigger and operator
cards.remember: Tag line keeps the load under control — never lift without one.

topics.title: Equipment & Machinery
topics.description: Mini excavators, trenchers, generators, and more
topics.intro: Outdoor lighting work means operating equipment. Know how each machine works and what it does best.

cards.title: Mini Excavator
list: Rental/company machine for digging trenches and holes
Controls: left stick = swing + boom; right stick = arm + bucket; pedals = tracks
Track or wheel: tracks better on soft ground, wheels faster on hard
Digging: use boom to position, arm to pull bucket through soil
Do not dig near utilities — hand dig within 24" of marked lines
Keep the machine level — use the blade to stabilize
Swing drive: watch counterweight clearance when rotating
cards.remember: Mini ex is for digging — not for lifting heavy loads with the bucket.

cards.title: Skid Steer
list: Versatile loader for grading, moving material, backfilling
Controls: joysticks or hand/foot — left drive right drive (tank steer)
Bucket for grading/loading — forks for pallets — auger for holes
Wheels or tracks: tracks better on soft ground
Never carry riders — they can fall into the machine
Keep ROPS up and seatbelt on at all times
Load capacity varies — check the plate
cards.remember: Skid steer = material moving — not a people hauler.

cards.title: Trencher
list: Purpose: cutting narrow trenches for conduit and cable
Walk-behind for small jobs (18-24" deep), ride-on for larger
Chain-type: chain with teeth digs through soil and rock
Wheel-type: wheel with cutting teeth for shallow, wide trenches
Call 811 before ANY trenching — no exceptions
Mark utility lines — trencher will destroy unmarked lines
Keep hands and feet away from cutting chain — it will pull you in
cards.remember: Trencher cuts fast — call 811 and mark ALL utilities first.

cards.title: Generators (Construction)
list: Portable generators for temporary power
Size: total running watts + 25% for startup surge
Ground the generator per NEC — use a grounding rod
Never run indoors or in enclosed space — CO poisoning kills
Use proper extension cords rated for load
Fuel: gasoline, diesel, or propane — diesel most common for large
Maintain fuel levels — running dry damages injectors on diesel
cards.remember: Generator + CO = deadly — always run outdoors with ventilation.

cards.title: Cable Tugger (Setup & Use)
list: Position in line with conduit pull direction
Anchor to truck, beam, or ground using straps/chains
Set max tension to wire rating — do not exceed
Pull speed: steady and slow — jerking damages wire
Operator monitors tension gauge — stop if it spikes
Feed end: one person feeds wire with lube
Communication: clear commands to tugger operator
cards.remember: Tugger pulls are powerful — never stand in line with a pull under tension.

cards.title: Hydraulic Crimper
list: Used for crimping lugs on #6 to 750 kcmil+ wire
Interchangeable dies must match lug size exactly
Pump types: hand, battery, or electric
Battery crimpers are fast — common on commercial/industrial
Crimp twice for lugs rated for dual indents
Pull test after crimp — wire should not pull out of lug
Keep dies clean — dirt = weak crimp
cards.remember: Die must match lug perfectly — wrong die = bad crimp = fire risk.

topics.title: Lighting Systems
topics.description: Sports fields, parking lots, photocells, and controls
topics.intro: Lighting is the most visible part of an electrical job. Good lighting work gets you called back for the next project.

cards.title: Outdoor Lighting Overview
list: Types: sports field, parking lot, wall packs, flood lights, bollards
Mounting: pole mounted, wall mounted, ground mounted
Control: photocell, time clock, contactor, smart controls
Light source: LED is standard now — HID (metal halide) being phased out
cards.remember: LED = today's standard. HID = old tech still found in retrofits.

cards.title: Sports Field Lighting
list: High-mast poles: 40-80 ft tall with multiple fixture banks
Requires engineered foundation and anchor bolt template
Each fixture bank aimed at specific zone on field
Light level measured in foot-candles — varies by sport level
Controls: typically photocell + time clock + contactor
Dimming for different events (practice vs game)
Emergency generator backup for safety lighting
cards.remember: Field lighting is precision — aim matters as much as power.

cards.title: Parking Lot Lighting
list: Standard pole heights: 20-40 ft
Fixture cutoff type matters — full cutoff reduces light trespass
Zoning: perimeter, aisle, and canopy zones have different requirements
Pole spacing based on fixture pattern and desired foot-candles
Photocell on each fixture or group control
Pole base with handhole adjacent for pull access
cards.remember: Parking lot lighting = even coverage without dark spots.

cards.title: Photocells
list: Light-sensitive switch — turns lights on at dusk, off at dawn
Types: stem-mounted on fixture, integral (in-fixture), remote (on panel)
Test: cover sensor to simulate dark — lights should come on
Common problem: sensors fail in 'on' or 'off' position
Nighttime troubleshooting: aim flashlight at sensor to simulate daylight
Orientation: should face north to avoid vehicle headlight interference
cards.remember: Photocell north-facing = fewer false triggers from headlights.

cards.title: Contactors (Lighting Control)
list: Contactor = big relay for switching multiple circuits at once
Coil voltage: 24V, 120V, 208V, 240V, 277V — must match control circuit
Use contactor when switching multiple lights or high load
Mechanically held contactors stay closed (no coil hum)
Always wire coil per manufacturer diagram
Lighting contactors are in a dedicated enclosure (often gray)
cards.remember: Photo cell or time clock triggers the contactor coil — contactor does the heavy switching.

cards.title: Time Clocks
list: Mechanical or digital timer that switches lights on/off at set times
Astronomical time clock: adjusts for sunrise/sunset automatically
Battery backup: maintains schedule during power outage
Set time of day and on/off events
Override switch for manual control during maintenance
Common on parking lot and sign lighting
cards.remember: Astronomical clocks adjust for seasons — best for outdoor lighting.

cards.title: LED Retrofits
list: Replace HID fixtures/bulbs with LED for energy savings
Retrofit kit: replaces bulb + ballast with LED driver + board
Compatibility: check that LED works with existing dimming/controls
Color temperature: 3000K (warm), 4000K (neutral), 5000K (daylight)
Wattage reduction: typical 50-70% savings vs HID
Wiring: bypass ballast — wire line to LED driver directly
cards.remember: LED retrofits pay for themselves in energy savings — know how to bypass ballasts.

cards.title: Pole Bases & Handholes (Detail)
list: Pole base: concrete poured to engineered spec
Anchor bolts: 4-bolt pattern — template must be level and plumb
Stub-up: PVC conduit from handhole to pole interior
Ground: grounding lug in pole base — bond pole to GEC
Handhole: access box adjacent to pole for pulling wire
Wire: feed in handhole, pull through stub-up into pole
Seal: duct seal around wires entering pole — prevent moisture
cards.remember: Pole base = template accuracy ± 1/4" — once concrete is poured, there is no adjustment.

cards.title: Underground Feeds for Lighting
list: PVC conduit from source to each pole/light location
Minimum 18" cover for residential, 24" under paved areas
Pull boxes at direction changes and long straight runs
Wire: THWN (wet rated) for underground conduit
Loop feed: wire runs pole-to-pole in continuous conduit
Tee feed: wire splits at handhole to multiple poles
Label circuits at both ends
cards.remember: Underground lighting feeds = THWN in PVC with pull boxes at every turn.

cards.title: 480V Lighting
list: 277/480V systems use 277V phase-to-neutral for lighting
Lighter wire gauge for same wattage vs 120V (lower current)
Typical in big-box stores, warehouses, industrial facilities
Fixtures must be rated for 277V
Switching: 277V rated switches and contactors required
Safety: 277V can kill — LOTO and confirm voltage before touching
cards.remember: 277V = commercial lighting voltage — higher voltage, smaller wire, same safety risk.

topics.title: Troubleshooting
topics.description: Photocells, open neutrals, breakers, and multimeter skills
topics.intro: Troubleshooting is 90% thinking and 10% testing. Follow the path, check voltages, and don't swap parts until you understand the problem.

cards.title: Troubleshooting Mindset
list: Do not guess — follow the circuit path
Start at the source and work toward the load
Ask: What should be happening? What is actually happening?
Divide the system in half — narrow the fault location
Voltage does not lie — let your meter tell the story
Check the simple things first (breaker, switch, connection)
cards.remember: You fix what you understand. You guess at what you do not.

cards.title: Bad Photocell
list: Symptoms: lights stay on all day, or never come on at night
Test: cover photocell completely — lights should turn on
If lights do not come on: photocell may be failed, or no power to circuit
If lights stay on in daylight: photocell is stuck closed (failed)
Check for loose neutral — photocells need neutral to operate
Note: some photocells have a delay (1-5 min) — wait before diagnosing
cards.remember: Cover photocell → lights on? Photocell is good. No change? Photocell or power problem.

cards.title: Open Neutral
list: Symptoms: lights dim/bright randomly, voltages fluctuate, electronics damaged
On a 120V circuit: hot-neutral reads 0V, hot-ground reads 120V
On MWBC: 240V across legs, 120V loads get 120-180V frying electronics
Danger: open neutral in MWBC = 240V on 120V devices — instant damage
Find: check all neutral connections in boxes, panels, and devices
Fix: tighten or replace wire nut on neutral bundle
cards.remember: Open neutral = weird voltages = instant equipment damage.

cards.title: Open Circuit (No Power)
list: Check breaker — tripped?
Check GFCI — tripped?
Check switch — working?
Test voltage at closest upstream device
Work backward from dead device to last working device
Check for loose connections, cut wires, or rodent damage
Test continuity on switches (power OFF)
cards.remember: Dead outlet + neighbors working? Check connections at the working outlet — it feeds the dead one.

cards.title: Bad Breaker
list: Signs: breaker trips immediately, will not reset, or trips under normal load
Test: swap with same type breaker from another slot (power OFF)
If the problem moves with the breaker = bad breaker
If the problem stays on the same circuit = wiring issue
Never replace a breaker with higher amp rating — wire must match
Arc fault breakers are sensitive — nuisance trips possible
cards.remember: Swap test: move breaker to different slot to confirm bad vs good.

cards.title: Voltage Checks (Systematic)
list: Step 1: Test main lugs — power coming into building?
Step 2: Test main breaker output — main breaker good?
Step 3: Test branch breaker — power leaving panel?
Step 4: Test at first device on circuit
Step 5: Test at each device working toward the dead one
Record readings at each step — compare to expected
Always test hot-neutral AND hot-ground AND neutral-ground
cards.remember: Systematic voltage checks find the break every time — skip steps at your own risk.

cards.title: Multimeter Basics for Troubleshooting
list: AC voltage: V~ with wavy line — outlets, panels, switches
DC voltage: V with straight/dashed line — batteries, sensors
Resistance: Ω — heaters, coils, motor windings (power OFF)
Continuity: beep symbol — wires, fuses, switches (power OFF)
Clamp meter: measures current without breaking circuit
Frequency: Hz — VFD output, generator frequency
cards.remember: Wrong setting = wrong reading = wrong diagnosis — confirm mode before probing.

cards.title: Continuity Testing
list: Power OFF — always — or you blow the meter fuse
Touch probes together — should beep (good meter)
Test: one probe each end of wire — beep = good path
Test: switch across terminals — beep when on, no beep when off
Test: fuse across ends — beep = good, no beep = blown
Test: heater element across terminals — low ohms = good
OL = open. 0Ω = short. Both mean something is wrong
cards.remember: Power OFF before continuity — never test continuity on a live circuit.

cards.title: Reading Schematics & One-Lines
list: One-line: shows power flow from utility to load — not physical layout
Schematic: shows how components connect and operate
Follow voltage left to right on schematics
Identify: source, switch, load, and return path
Labels: wire numbers match terminal numbers on devices
For troubleshooting: find the device that is not getting power
cards.remember: Schematic = logic. One-line = power path. Both help you find the break.

cards.title: Troubleshooting Flow (The 7 Steps)
list: 1. Identify the problem — what is not working?
2. Understand the circuit — what should be happening?
3. Check the obvious — tripped breaker? tripped GFCI? dead switch?
4. Measure voltage at the source and work outward
5. Isolate — what part of the system works vs does not work?
6. Test component — continuity, resistance, or suspect device swap
7. Fix and verify — repair, restore power, confirm operation
cards.remember: Step 3 (check the obvious) solves 50% of problems — do not skip it.

topics.title: YouTube University
topics.description: Best channels and videos for apprentices
topics.intro: The best electricians never stop learning. These YouTube channels teach everything from theory to field tricks.

cards.title: Electrician U
list: Dustin Stelzer — excellent for exam prep and field knowledge
Tons of walk-throughs, code questions, and real-world scenarios
Great for apprentice and journeyman exam study
Search: 'Electrician U conduit bending', 'Electrician U grounding'
Best starter: 'Electrical Basics — Everything You Need to Know'
cards.remember: Electrician U = best all-around channel for exam prep.

cards.title: The Engineering Mindset
list: Best for understanding electrical THEORY visually
Animated explanations of voltage, current, AC/DC, transformers
Great 3D animations show electron flow clearly
Titles: 'How Electricity Works', 'How Transformers Work', 'AC vs DC'
Not field-focused — pure science and engineering
cards.remember: Engineering Mindset = theory made visual — watch before your exam.

cards.title: Mike Holt (NEC)
list: Mike Holt is the authority on the National Electrical Code
Code training videos, podcasts, and free resources
Best for: understanding CODE, not just how-to
Watch: 'Grounding vs Bonding' — most important NEC topic
His website/app is a study tool too
cards.remember: Mike Holt = go-to for code answers — practical theory.

cards.title: Essential Craftsman
list: Not electrical-specific — but the BEST channel for trade mindset
Scott Wadsworth teaches work ethic, professionalism, and construction
Watch: 'The Spec House' series — full construction build
Also: '7 Things You Need to Know Before Starting Construction'
Life lessons every apprentice needs to hear
cards.remember: Essential Craftsman = mindset and work ethic — every apprentice should watch.

cards.title: Sparky Channel
list: Real electrician doing residential and commercial work
Good for watching actual installs and methods
See how pros do rough-in, trim-out, panel work
Learn tips for everyday electrical tasks
Practical, not overly produced
cards.remember: Sparky Channel = watch real work being done — learn by seeing.

cards.title: Daily Study Plan for YouTube
cards.remember: 30 min daily = 182 hours of learning in a year.

cards.title: Other Great Channels
list: MAKE: electronics for understanding how components work
EEVBLOG: deep dives on electronics engineering
ElectroBOOM: funny but educational — safety awareness
Southwire: manufacturer training videos
Klein Tools: tool usage and techniques
Industrial Control Wizard: PLC and motor control
cards.remember: Bookmark the channels that match what you are studying right now.

cards.title: How to Use YouTube Effectively
list: Do not just watch — take notes. Write down key facts.
Pause and rewind on bending and wiring — watch multiple times
Create a playlist for each topic (theory, bending, code)
Watch the comment section — pros add tips and corrections
Follow up by looking up the code article referenced
Practice what you watch — knowledge without practice fades
cards.remember: Video shows you how. Your hands teach you why. Practice both.
